sites.name: Spittal Pond Nature Reserve
sites.access: Free, dawn to dusk; two small car parks on South Road.
sites.kids: A loop trail of about a mile with cows on one side and the ocean on the other. Bring binoculars.
sites.see: Herons, egrets and winter ducks on the pond; Portuguese Rock on the cliff, with its early carved date; the flat checkerboard rock by the sea.
sites.story: The largest nature reserve on the island and the best single place for birds, run by the National Trust and the Government. Migrating birds stop here in autumn and winter.
links: The Bermudian, A Walk in the Park
The Bermudian, The Bermuda National Trust Became the Largest Landowner
sections: Three things on the cliff
Portuguese Rock carries initials and the date 1543, cut by a shipwrecked sailor. The carving is now cast in bronze.
The Chequerboard is a flat floor of limestone scored into squares.
Jeffrey's Hole is a cave where an enslaved man named Jeffrey hid for several weeks after escaping.
How it was saved
Dr Henry Wilkinson deeded the western part of the pond and its shore to the Historical Monuments Trust in 1950.

sites.name: Bermuda Botanical Gardens
sites.access: Free, sunrise to sunset; entrances on South Road, Berry Hill Road and Point Finger Road.
sites.kids: Big lawns to run on, a maze, a sensory garden and banyan trees to climb under.
sites.see: The palm collection, the hibiscus garden, the old greenhouses, Camden House and the Masterworks Museum of Bermuda Art inside the grounds.
sites.story: Thirty six acres of gardens that have been public since Victorian times, and the home of the annual Agricultural Exhibition.

sites.name: The Arboretum
sites.access: Free, sunrise to sunset; Middle Road and Montpelier Road.
sites.kids: Wide open meadows and easy woodland paths, good for a first walk.
sites.see: Collections of trees from around the world, open meadow and bluebirds in the nest boxes.
sites.story: A quiet woodland park on former army land, planted as a tree collection.

sites.name: Blue Hole Park and Walsingham
sites.access: Free; park by the causeway at Blue Hole Hill and walk in. Paths are rough and rocky.
sites.kids: An adventure walk for older children: caves, pools and mangroves. Keep hold of little ones near the water and the cave mouths.
sites.see: Caves and grottoes with clear water, mangrove ponds, and the woodland people call Tom Moore's Jungle.
sites.story: Limestone caves and sinkholes hidden in the trees between Castle Harbour and Harrington Sound. The Irish poet Thomas Moore wrote here in 1804, which is where the nickname comes from.
links: The Bermudian, A Walk in the Park
sections: Dolphins and caves
Blue Hole was once a dolphin show. The dolphins are buried in a small cemetery nearby.
One cave mouth is framed by stalactites shaped like anteaters. A small bridge is a good place to watch parrotfish and sergeant majors.

sites.name: Paget Marsh Nature Reserve
sites.access: Free; a boardwalk from Lover's Lane, off South Road.
sites.kids: A short, flat boardwalk, easy with a pushchair, into a forest that looks prehistoric.
sites.see: Bermuda palmettos and cedars growing as they did before people arrived, with herons in the pond.
sites.story: One of the last scraps of the island's original forest, cared for by the National Trust and the Audubon Society.

sites.name: Nonsuch Island
sites.access: By guided boat tour only; it is a protected reserve with no casual landing.
sites.kids: Seen on a tour, and the cahow nest camera is online for the rest of the year.
sites.see: The cahow, Bermuda's national bird, which nests in burrows here from autumn to early summer.
sites.story: A 14 acre island at the east entrance to Castle Harbour, restored over more than sixty years into a living museum of Bermuda as the first settlers found it. It is the centre of the effort that brought the cahow back after it was thought extinct for three centuries.
links: Government of Bermuda, 2024 cahow nesting season
The Bermudian, David Wingate: A Life in Service to Bermuda's Natural World
sections: Before the museum
1865: a quarantine hospital for yellow fever. A small cemetery from those years remains on the eastern side.
1930: the base for William Beebe and Otis Barton's bathysphere dives.
By the 1950s the island was almost bare. A scale insect had killed Bermuda's cedars.
The living museum
1961: Nonsuch was declared a nature reserve, and David Wingate, newly married, moved out to live there as its caretaker.
He replanted it with native and endemic trees and plants, by hand, over decades, so that one corner of Bermuda would look as it did before people came.
The West Indian topshell was brought back here, and the island became the model for restoring habitat elsewhere in Bermuda.
The cahows
Chicks were moved here from the low outer islets from 2004 so that the birds would nest above the reach of hurricanes.
2009: the first cahow chick hatched on Nonsuch since the 1620s.
2024: 25 chicks fledged from Nonsuch, which made it the most productive of the nesting islands.
More of its story
The island is on Richard Norwood's map of the early 1600s. The Government bought it in 1865 for the yellow fever hospital, which moved to Coney Island early in the 1900s.
In 1928 it was lent for three years to the New York Zoological Society, and William Beebe and John Tee Van ran a marine research station here.
From 1934 it was a training school for boys, for about fourteen years, until the school moved to Paget Island.
The wreck off the north side is HMS Supply, a Navy water barge. She was turned into Bermuda's first glass bottomed boat, and Beebe had her sunk as a breakwater. Snorkellers can swim through her.
What Wingate put back
Between 1963 and 1972 he planted more than 8,000 native trees and shrubs. Of 600 cedars planted in 1972, about 200 lived.
In 1975 he dug a freshwater pond and a salt marsh.
Yellow crowned night herons: 44 nestlings were brought from Tampa Bay between 1976 and 1978 and reared here. They were nesting across the island by 1987.
West Indian top shells: 82 were put back in 1982. They were breeding by 1987 and have since spread round all of Bermuda.
Green turtles: about 16,000 were hatched and released between 1968 and 1978.
sites.camp: No. It is a closed nature reserve, seen by arranged tour only.

sites.name: Southlands Park
sites.era: Old estate, now a public park
sites.access: Free; off South Road, with paths down to the beach.
sites.kids: Giant banyan trees to explore and a walk that ends at the sea.
sites.see: The banyan grove, old quarry gardens, the ruins of the estate buildings, and one of the Invader mosaics by the beach.
sites.story: Thirty seven acres of woodland on the Warwick south shore, saved from development and made a public park. The estate goes back to the 1700s, when it was the home of the ministers of Christ Church, Warwick.
links: The Bermudian, Exploring Bermuda's Outdoor Places and Spaces
sections: Quarries and ruins
In the 1800s the land was quarried, and its limestone went into many buildings in Hamilton. The old quarries later became sunken gardens.
The houses of the estate now stand in ruins under ferns and moss. There is a tomb on the grounds, that of an owner, James Morgan, and his wife.
The park runs down to Marley Beach. It is open to the public but not maintained, so wear proper shoes.

sites.name: Victoria Park
sites.access: Free; in the City of Hamilton between Victoria, Cedar, Dundonald and Washington Streets.
sites.kids: A shady city park with room to run and a bandstand to climb around.
sites.see: The ornate cast iron bandstand put up for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee.
sites.story: Hamilton's formal garden, used for concerts and events.

sites.name: Crystal and Fantasy Caves
sites.access: Paid entry, guided tours daily; Wilkinson Avenue, off Harrington Sound Road.
sites.kids: A floating walkway over a clear underground lake. There are a lot of steps down and back up.
sites.see: Stalactites and soda straws above water so clear you can see the bottom far below.

sections: What is Bermuda made of? A long argument

Bermuda's caves and quarries puzzled scientists for a century. In 1833 a young army engineer, Richard Nelson, who had crawled through caves across the island, told the Geological Society in London that Bermuda had built up slowly from the remains of living things.

Charles Darwin never came here, but he wondered about the place and decided it was an odd sort of coral island that had formed as the sea floor sank. Americans who did come, Dana in the 1870s, Rice, Heilprin in 1888 and Agassiz in 1894, argued over how much was sinking, how much was coral and how much was wind and waves.

In the 1930s Robert Sayles of Harvard read the layers in the quarries and tied the island's dunes to the ice ages and the rise and fall of the sea. William Beebe, working here at the same time, thought each of them had been partly right.
In the 1970s two Yale scientists compared coral in dredged Castle Harbour with the outer reef and found far less alive in the harbour.
Other caves, and who they are for

Admiral's Cave, up the hill from the Swizzle Inn, is the opposite of Crystal: no lights, no railings, no guide. You go down a rope, and there are sharp, slippery drops into sea lakes. For the experienced only, never alone.
Grotto Bay's cave is a lit swimming hole with a walkway and a ladder, open to guests of the resort.
Church Cave, on the Rosewood's land, holds the largest underground lake in Bermuda. You need permission.
Sears Cave is a collapsed cave that makes a shaded sinkhole full of rare ferns. Once a rubbish dump. By appointment only, and the edge is unfenced.
Subway Cave at Walsingham is dry, hidden, and mostly a crawl. For practised cavers.
Green Bay Cave on Harrington Sound runs for more than two kilometres under water. Its drowned stalagmites show it was dry in the Ice Age. Certified cave divers only.

sections: Mr Mowbray's fish house

Louis L. Mowbray was born in St George's in 1877 and taught at home by his father. He worked on a pilot boat, ran a photography studio, and in 1904 was asked to join the visiting scientists at Flatts, where he organised daily trips to the reef.
In 1906, exploring Castle Island, he found a petrel he took for a new species. Years later it proved to be the cahow, long thought extinct.
After running Bermuda's first aquarium on Agar's Island he left in 1911 to build and run aquariums in Boston, New York and Miami.
Flatts, 1928
In 1925 the Assembly voted 12,800 pounds to build an aquarium at Flatts with Mowbray as curator. It opened on 1 February 1928 and had about 40,000 visitors by 1930.
It had a fish hatchery, gardens and its own expedition boat, the Iridio, and from the 1930s visitors could walk the floor of Harrington Sound in a diving helmet.
Money for a museum and zoo followed in 1936. Vincent Astor supplied animals, among them Galapagos tortoises.

Mowbray fell ill in 1943 and died in June 1952. His son Louis, assistant curator from the day it opened, took over in 1948 and ran it into the late 1960s. He was in the party that found the cahow alive in 1951.
With children on a wet day
The aquarium hall and the natural history museum are under cover, so this is the island's first choice when it rains. Allow two to three hours. The zoo outside is there if it clears.

sites.parish: Hamilton Parish and Smith's, at Flatts Inlet

sites.story: A small village with a long memory. It was settled in 1612, its footbridge may have been the first bridge in Bermuda, the Governor's Council once met here, and for two centuries its sheltered inlet was a smugglers' harbour.
sections: The bridge
A footbridge over the tidal race is mentioned in the Assembly's minutes for 1620. In 1718 a man was punished on it for blasphemy.
Paintings of 1823 show a flimsy wooden thing, and in 1827 it was declared too dangerous to cross. It could be taken out to let a ship through: a notice of 1833 gives the charge as ten shillings.
Bridge House
A house by the bridge is on record from 1681. The Governor's Council met there in 1696 and from 1702 to 1709, and later the assize court sat there.

Augustus Peniston bought the present house in 1822. In 1844 it became a receiving office, an early branch post office, on the mail coach road between Hamilton and St George's. In 1920 it was bought by the parents of Sir Henry Tucker, who became Bermuda's first Government Leader.
Smugglers and merchants

In the 1600s and 1700s ships slipped into the inlet to dodge the customs officer at St George's. The trade faded once Hamilton became the port of entry. Stanley House, built in the middle of the 1700s, still has the deep cellars.
The Musson family built many of the stone houses and warehouses. One of them, Susanna Musson, known as Captain Sukey, owned ships and a shop and died with money hidden about her house.
Wistowe

John Walker built the first house here and used the tide race to turn a mill that ground aloes. In 1741 a duel was fought on the property: Peter Nice was killed and Robert Hill sentenced to death, then pardoned.
After 1865 it was the home of the American consul, Charles Maxwell Allen, and Mark Twain was among his guests. The radio pioneer Reginald Fessenden lived here from 1928 to 1932.
Hotels, fish and trains

The Mussons' big house became the Frascati Hotel at the start of the 1900s. American servicemen danced there in the Second World War, and it ended as the Coral Island Hotel. St James Court stands on the site.
The Aquarium arrived in the 1920s and the railway in 1931, with a stop at the Aquarium.

A handful of Bermudians set up the Historical Monuments Trust in 1937 to rescue old buildings. Tucker House was the first thing it bought, in 1939, for 800 pounds.

Stewart Hall, Buckingham, Fanny Fox's Cottage, the Old Rectory and the Globe Hotel followed through the 1940s. The National Trust took over the work under an Act of 1969 and is now the largest landowner on the island.

sections: Who built it and who lived there
In the 1600s the land belonged to William Sayle, who later left to become the first Governor of South Carolina.

The house was built for John Dickinson, a shipowner and Speaker of the House of Assembly from 1707 to 1710. It was built and kept up by enslaved people for more than 125 years, until Emancipation. Dickinson held six people in the early 1700s. By the early 1800s fourteen enslaved people lived here.
Inside
Cedar and mahogany furniture, English and Chinese porcelain, Georgian silver made in Bermuda, children's furniture and toys, and a cedar staircase.
The magazine lists guided tours on Fridays and every second Saturday. Check with the Trust before you go. 6 Verdmont Lane, off Collector's Hill.
How it was saved
Around 1951 the house was offered to the Historical Monuments Trust on generous terms. Its members judged it probably the finest house of its period in Bermuda, and almost unaltered.

sections: The Boer War islands
About 5,000 Boer prisoners were shipped to Bermuda during the South African War and held on small islands in the Great Sound in 1901 and 1902.
They were sorted by their views. Those who wanted to fight on went to Darrell's Island.
A newspaper of the time counted 884 men on Morgan's Island, 809 on Tucker's, 607 on Burt's and 35 on Ports Island, where the hospital was.
Long Island belonged to the Admiralty and was one of the camps. Its cemetery, first used by the military for victims of yellow fever, became the Boer cemetery.
When peace came the prisoners put up an obelisk here to their dead. The Bermuda National Trust keeps the cemetery as a memorial.

sites.name: BIOS, the Bermuda Institute of Ocean Sciences
sites.access: 25 Biological Station, Ferry Reach. A working research station, not a visitor attraction, with office hours on weekdays. Watch for open house days, when the public can tour the labs and the ship.
sites.see: The research ship at the dock, seen from the road along Ferry Reach.
sites.story: One of the oldest ocean research stations in the western hemisphere, and since 2021 part of Arizona State University. Its long records of the sea off Bermuda are used by climate scientists all over the world.
sections: What they measure
Hydrostation S: the temperature and salt of the deep ocean, sampled every two weeks since 1954. It is the longest running record of its kind in the world.
BATS, the Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study: the physics, chemistry and biology of the Sargasso Sea, sampled every month since 1988.
The Oceanic Flux Program: what sinks from the surface to the deep sea.
Why it matters

Because the same spot has been sampled for decades, these records show how the ocean is warming, turning more acidic and changing its life. Professor Nicholas Bates at BIOS is known for his work on ocean carbon and acidification.

sections: Artemis II, April 2026
When four astronauts lifted off for a ten day trip round the Moon on 1 April 2026, the launch was monitored from Cooper's Island. Guests watched from the station, and cheers went up at lift off.
Kimille Trott, a Bermudian engineer on the Artemis programme, followed the launch from a console at the Marshall Space Flight Centre in Alabama.
What may come next
In 2026 the UK Space Agency applied for planning permission to put three telescopes on Cooper's Island, to help track objects in orbit.
The agreement that let NASA return was extended in 2017 to run until 2026. The Hub has not found a report of what follows it.

sites.access: BIOS, Ferry Reach. A working research station, closed to the public outside open days.

sites.story: Who is doing the science at Ferry Reach right now, and what each of them studies. Names and roles come from BIOS and Arizona State University pages.
sections: Leading the institute

Craig Carlson, director since 2025 and a professor of microbial oceanography. He first came to the station as a visiting researcher in the late 1980s and joined its faculty in the 1990s. In November 2026 he was named chair elect of the body that coordinates the American research fleet.
The ocean record keepers
Nicholas Bates, senior scientist and director of research, leads BATS, the monthly sampling of the Sargasso Sea that began in 1988. He is known for work on ocean carbon and acidification.
Rod Johnson is his partner on BATS. Together they reported that over the life of the record the surface sea off Bermuda has warmed by about 1 degree Celsius and become about 30 per cent more acidic.
Plankton and the twilight zone
Amy Maas, a biological oceanographer, studies plankton and the dim middle depths of the ocean, including with NASA.
Leocadio Blanco-Bercial works with her on the tiny animals called copepods that swim up and down through the water every day.
Reefs
Eric Hochberg, a reef systems ecologist, measures coral reefs by the light they reflect and has mapped how much coral covers Bermuda's reefs.
Samantha de Putron teaches and helps run the university programmes that bring students to work on the reefs.
Weather and risk
Mark Guishard wrote the BIOS report on the impacts and risks of climate change for Bermuda.

sites.name: Henry Stommel and Hydrostation S
sites.access: The station is a patch of open ocean about 25 km south east of Bermuda. The ship that visits it sails from BIOS at Ferry Reach.
sites.see: Nothing marks the spot. The Atlantic Explorer card on the Ocean tab shows the next Hydrostation S trip.
sites.story: The longest running record of the deep ocean anywhere in the world began off Bermuda in 1954, and it has not stopped since.
sections: How it began
Henry Stommel of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution set it up with William Sutcliffe, then director of the Bermuda Biological Station.
Every two weeks a small wooden research boat, the Panulirus, went out to the same spot to measure temperature, salt and oxygen all the way down. The station was first known by the boat's name.
Who was Stommel
One of the great ocean scientists of the last century, and unusual in becoming a full professor without ever earning a doctorate.
His honours included the Crafoord Prize in 1983 and the United States National Medal of Science in 1989.
Why it still matters
Because the same water has been measured for seven decades, the record shows the ocean changing. It led directly to BATS in 1988, and both are still sampled from the Atlantic Explorer today.

sites.name: Louis Mowbray, the man who built the Aquarium

sites.kids: A good story for the Aquarium: it was built by a St George's boy who taught himself.
sites.see: The aquarium he designed and ran.
sites.story: A largely self taught Bermudian naturalist who became known abroad for designing and running aquariums, then came home to build one in Flatts and ran it for nearly twenty years.
sections: His life
Born in St George's on 19 August 1877. As a teenager he was helmsman of a pilot gig, racing to guide ships into port.
Visiting scientists were so impressed that they invited him on to the staff of the Bermuda Biological Station, which began in 1903 at the Frascati Hotel in Flatts.
He was the first curator of the Bermuda Aquarium until poor health made him retire in 1944. He died on 5 June 1952.
Mowbray and the cahow
In 1906 he found a live cahow, a bird believed extinct for centuries, and in 1916 he helped describe it for science.
His son, also Louis Mowbray, was on the 1951 expedition that found the birds nesting, with the schoolboy David Wingate along.
Firsts
He bred Galapagos tortoises and penguins in captivity, both rare achievements for the time.

sites.name: Cave life: Tom Iliffe and Wolfgang Sterrer
sites.access: The Walsingham caves lie under Blue Hole Park and Tom Moore's Jungle. See caves safely at Crystal and Fantasy Caves or from the park trails.
sites.see: Still, clear pools at cave mouths along the Walsingham trails. The animals that made them famous are tiny and live deep inside.
sites.story: Bermuda's flooded caves hold animals found nowhere else on Earth, and nobody had looked until a curious question was asked at the Biological Station.
sections: The question

Tom Iliffe, then at the Bermuda Biological Station, wondered why the cave pools seemed empty and asked its director, Wolfgang Sterrer, whether anyone had ever searched the saltwater caves for animals.
Nobody had. From 1980 Iliffe and Sterrer dived and collected, and new species followed one after another.
What they found
Shrimps, worms and other small animals new to science. Some carry the island's name, such as the cave shrimp Bermudacaris, and one is named for Sterrer himself.
Some have their closest relatives in Pacific caves or the deep sea, a puzzle about how they ever reached Bermuda.
A 2021 study called the Walsingham caves a global hotspot for animals that live only in such caves. Many are listed as critically endangered.
The two scientists
Iliffe went on to Texas A and M University and became a leading cave biologist.
Sterrer became curator of the Bermuda Natural History Museum at the Aquarium, where he is now curator emeritus. His own speciality is the tiny animals that live between grains of sand.

sites.name: David Wingate (1935 to 2026)
sites.access: His life's work is Nonsuch Island, a closed nature reserve seen by arranged tour. The pin marks the island.
sites.kids: Tell the story of the schoolboy who helped find a bird everyone thought was gone for ever, then watch the CahowCam.
sites.see: Nonsuch Island itself: every tree on it was planted in his time.
sites.story: Bermuda's first Conservation Officer, and the man who brought the cahow back. David Balcombe Wingate was born on 11 October 1935 and died on 10 November 2026, aged 91. For more than seventy years he was the person the island asked about its plants, birds and wild places.
sections: The boy on the expedition
A Saltus Grammar School pupil with a passion for natural history, he was 15 when he joined Louis Mowbray and Robert Cushman Murphy on the 1951 search of the Castle Roads islets.
They caught a live cahow on Inner Pear islet. The bird had been thought extinct for about 300 years, and 18 pairs were left.
A working life
1957: a degree in zoology from Cornell University. He took no further degrees, though he is often called Dr Wingate.
1961: moved to Nonsuch Island as its caretaker and pressed for it to be made a nature reserve, which happened that year.
1966: became Bermuda's first Conservation Officer.
2000: retired at 65. Jeremy Madeiros took over the cahow work.
What he left
The cahow: from 18 pairs to more than 160.
Nonsuch Island, replanted as a living museum of Bermuda before people.
Artificial burrows and other practical ways of protecting the nests.
A generation of Bermudian naturalists and the island's conservation community.
Remembering him
His family asked for donations to the Bermuda National Trust, the Bermuda Audubon Society, Buy Back Bermuda or the Warwick Academy Natural History Club.
The 2006 documentary Rare Bird, by Lucinda Spurling, tells the story.
Life on the island
When he moved to Nonsuch the warden's cottage, part of the old quarantine hospital, had no telephone and no electricity.
By the early 1990s about 3,000 people a year were visiting, many of them schoolchildren.

sites.name: The cahow comeback
sites.access: Nonsuch Island is a closed nature reserve. Visits are by arranged tour only. Anyone can watch the nest cameras online.
sites.kids: Watch the CahowCam together: the birds come back in October and the chicks hatch from February.
sites.story: The cahow, or Bermuda petrel, is the national bird and one of the rarest seabirds on Earth. It was thought extinct for about 300 years until 1951, when Louis Mowbray and the American seabird expert Robert Cushman Murphy searched the Castle Roads islets with 15 year old David Wingate and caught a live bird on Inner Pear islet, off St David's.
sections: The numbers
18 pairs were all that survived when the bird was found again.
Around 1960, when active protection began, those 17 or 18 pairs raised only 7 or 8 chicks a year between them.
2009: the first chick hatched on Nonsuch Island since the 1620s.
2022: 156 breeding pairs and 77 chicks fledged.
2023: 164 breeding pairs and 76 chicks, nesting on six islands that total 22.5 acres.
2024: 76 chicks across the colony, 25 of them on Nonsuch, the island's best year to that date.
The 2026 count on this page was 166 breeding pairs.
The recovery
David Wingate began protecting the nests around 1960 and gave his working life to it. He died on 10 November 2026, aged 91.

Jeremy Madeiros took over when Wingate retired in 2000, and from 2004 moved chicks to Nonsuch Island so the birds would nest on higher, safer ground again. The chicks were fed by hand in concrete burrows until they flew, so that they would come back to Nonsuch to breed.
About half of the moved chicks have returned.
The season
The birds return to their burrows in October and November, lay a single egg around January, and the chicks hatch from mid February and fly in late spring.
Half a million birds
When Spanish and Portuguese sailors first came by in the early 1500s there were something like half a million cahows. Their night calls helped keep those sailors from settling.
Pigs put ashore by passing ships began the slaughter. The English added dogs, cats and rats, and by about 1620 the bird was thought to be gone.
How the move to Nonsuch was done
Jeremy Madeiros learned the method in Australia from the biologist Nicholas Carlile. In 2004 the first 14 chicks were moved to Nonsuch before they could fly, so that they would remember it as home.
The first of them came back in February 2008. The first chick hatched there in 2009 and was named Somers.
Young males take three or four years to return after they first fly, and females four to six. A pair lays one egg a year, which is why recovery is slow.
At sea
Tracking tags show the birds range over three to four million square miles of the North Atlantic. An ordinary feeding trip is 2,500 to 3,500 miles. One bird went 10,000.
The CahowCam

Jean-Pierre Rouja built the first burrow camera from an action camera altered to see in infrared. Since 2013 cameras have streamed live from Nonsuch with the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, and people in more than 100 countries have watched.
What threatens them now
The sea. The original islets are low, and Madeiros expects at least three of the four to be unusable by the 2050s. Hurricane Fabian wrecked more than four in five of the concrete burrows.
The target is 1,000 pairs, hoped for around 2050, when the bird would no longer be listed as critically endangered.
A note on the numbers: accounts of how many pairs were found in 1951 differ. This magazine article says eight known pairs, and other sources say eighteen.

sites.name: Beebe's bathysphere dives
sites.access: Open sea, about five miles south east of Nonsuch Island. Nothing to see on the water: the story is the point.
sites.kids: Two men in a steel ball five feet across, with a window eight inches wide.
sites.story: The first time people saw the deep sea alive. William Beebe and Otis Barton were lowered on a cable from a ship off Nonsuch in a hollow steel ball called the bathysphere, with Beebe describing the glowing animals by telephone to Gloria Hollister on deck.
sections: The dives
22 September 1932: 2,100 feet, described live on NBC radio.
15 August 1934: 3,028 feet, more than half a mile down. The record stood for 15 years.
Beebe ran his field station on Nonsuch Island through these years.

sites.name: Coral gardens, Living Reefs Foundation
sites.access: The first gardens are in Castle Harbour, off Rosewood Bermuda. Workshops and adopt a coral garden places are booked through the foundation.
sites.story: Bermuda has the most northerly coral reefs in the Atlantic. The foundation, led by marine biologist Dr Samia Sarkis, raises young boulder corals from larvae in a hatchery and plants them in underwater gardens to repair damaged reef. The first garden went into Castle Harbour in August 2016.

sites.name: Bermuda Underwater Exploration Institute
sites.access: 40 Crow Lane, at the edge of Hamilton. Listed as open weekdays 10am to 5pm and weekends 10am to 4pm. Phone 441-292-7219.
sites.kids: An ocean discovery centre built for families.
sites.see: Shipwreck finds, shells and the deep sea.
sites.story: The ocean discovery centre on Hamilton Harbour. Beyond the exhibits it runs conservation work of its own, including a project to restore the seagrass meadows that Bermuda's young turtles feed on.
sections: With children on a wet day
Hands on displays and shipwreck stories, all indoors, a short walk from the centre of Hamilton. Allow about two hours.

sites.name: Hunting lionfish: the guide
sites.access: Anywhere in Bermuda waters, with a culling permit.
sites.see: Red and white stripes and long fan like fins, usually hanging still under a ledge.
sites.story: Lionfish come from the Indo Pacific and have almost no predators here. They eat young reef fish at a rate the reef cannot replace, breed all year, and live from the shallows down to 1,000 feet. Trained divers spearing them, one at a time, is still the best control there is.
sections: The permit

Residents can get a lionfish culling permit from the Bermuda Lionfish Task Force. It lets you carry a three prong sling spear, hunt on scuba, hunt within a mile of shore, and hunt on wrecks and protected sites, all of which are otherwise off limits for spearfishing. Training dates are posted on the culling programme's Facebook page. Visitors can take a lionfish culling course at the dive shops instead.
Best time
Dawn and dusk. That is when lionfish come out to feed, and when they are found in shallow water.
In the middle of the day they tuck in under overhangs and inside holes, so look there.
Best places
Most of Bermuda's lionfish live deep, on the reef slope from about 100 to 200 feet, which is why so many are caught in lobster traps.
In the shallows, hunters do best along the South Shore reefs at dusk, and on wrecks and ledges.
Lionfish are territorial. If you see one and miss it, it will very likely be in the same spot next time.
The task force map shows every sighting and catch by year, so you can see where others have found them.
Report every one
Report each lionfish you see or catch, with the place, on the task force website. Report trips where you saw none too: that tells the scientists where they are not.
Drop off for science
You can give your catch to the researchers at the Aquarium in Flatts, Marine Resources on Coney Island, Dive Bermuda at Grotto Bay or Blue Water Divers in Dockyard.
Tournaments
Winter Lionfish Derby: all of January, for permit holders. In 2026 more than 1,000 lionfish were caught.
Heatwave: a few days in August, with almost 50 teams in 2026.
Careful
A lionfish has 18 venomous spines. A sting is not deadly but is very painful.
The usual first aid is to soak the wound in water as hot as you can stand without burning, and to see a doctor.

sites.name: The Bermuda Triangle: the guide
sites.access: Albuoy's Point, on the Hamilton waterfront beside the ferry terminal. Open all the time and free.
sites.kids: Find the bronze marker in the triangular walkway and stand on the corner of the Triangle.
sites.see: The marker for the northern point of the Triangle, set into the paving of Point Pleasant Park.
sites.story: Bermuda is the top corner of the most famous patch of ocean in the world. The Triangle runs from here to Miami and to San Juan in Puerto Rico. Whether anything strange happens inside it is another matter, and the honest answer is below.
sections: Where the name came from
A writer called Vincent Gaddis coined it in 1964 in Argosy, an American pulp magazine. Charles Berlitz made it world famous with a 1974 book that blamed the lost city of Atlantis.
The two that left from here
Star Tiger, a British South American Airways airliner, vanished on 30 January 1948 on its way from the Azores to Kindley Field with about 30 people on board.
Star Ariel, her sister aircraft, took off from Kindley Field for Jamaica on 17 January 1949 with 20 people on board, reported good weather, and was never heard from again.
No wreckage from either was ever found. These two losses are a large part of why the Triangle carries Bermuda's name.
The other famous cases
USS Cyclops, 1918: a US Navy supply ship lost with 306 crew and no trace.
Flight 19, 1945: five Navy torpedo bombers that left Fort Lauderdale on a training flight and never came back.
What the experts say
The US Navy, the US Coast Guard and NOAA all say nothing supernatural is going on.
NOAA finds no more losses here than in any other busy stretch of ocean, and this is one of the busiest.
The usual suspects are the Gulf Stream, sudden storms and hurricanes, and rogue waves.
The real ship eater
Bermuda's own danger is the reef. More than 300 wrecks lie around the island, and you can dive or snorkel a good number of them. See Wrecks in Explore and Scuba in Sports.
Do the Triangle
Stand on the marker at Albuoy's Point.
See the exhibit at BUEI.
Go To Bermuda also lists a three scoop Bermuda Triangle ice cream at Meltdown and a restaurant called Lost in the Triangle. Check both are still going before you set out.

sites.name: Bermuda Triangle: Unlock the Secrets, at BUEI
sites.access: Inside the Ocean Discovery Centre at BUEI, 40 Crow Lane, about 15 minutes on foot from the Hamilton ferry. Listed as open weekdays 10am to 5pm and weekends 10am to 4pm. Phone 441-292-7219.
sites.kids: Built for them: a touch table, a sinking ship simulation and a Survive the Bermuda Triangle game.
sites.see: A touch table with the story of each lost ship and aircraft, a 3D hurricane hologram and the best known Triangle stories.
sites.story: The only permanent Bermuda Triangle exhibit there is, and it is in the right country. It lays out the disappearances and then the science that explains most of them.

sites.name: Star Tiger and Star Ariel, Kindley Field
sites.access: Kindley Field is today's L.F. Wade International Airport. There is nothing to visit for the two aircraft. This pin marks where one was due to land and the other took off.
sites.see: The runway both stories turn on.
sites.story: Two airliners of the same type and the same airline were lost within a year of each other, both on Bermuda flights. Star Tiger was inbound from the Azores on the night of 30 January 1948 and never arrived. Star Ariel left here for Kingston on the morning of 17 January 1949, radioed that she was flying in good visibility, and vanished. Neither sent a distress call and nothing was ever recovered.

sites.name: Ghost stories of Bermuda: the guide
sites.access: King's Square, St George's, where the Haunted History tour gathers.
sites.kids: The tour is theatre more than terror, but it runs after dark.
sites.see: Lantern light, capes and top hats in the back lanes of the old town.
sites.story: An island settled by shipwreck in 1609 collects ghosts. The stories here are folklore as local writers and the newspapers have told them. Nobody is promising you a sighting.
sections: Haunted History tour

Storytellers in period costume lead up to 25 people through the alleys of St George's for about an hour. Go To Bermuda lists it on Saturdays, 8:30pm in October and 7pm from November to March, starting at The Book Cellar, 5 Water Street. Adults $35, seniors and under 16s $25. Phone 441-705-1838. Check the time before you go.
The Isle of Devils

Old charts gave Bermuda that name, and for a century sailors kept clear. The usual explanation is the cahow, whose night calls sounded like demons to Spanish and Portuguese crews. See the cahow under Science and conservation.
Sally Bassett's flower
Sally Bassett was an enslaved woman burned at the stake at Crow Lane. Legend says the first Bermudiana, the island's small purple flower, grew from her ashes.
Private houses, so stories only
Orange Valley, Devonshire: footsteps, a hand on the shoulder, and a silent woman in a long dress pointing at the place where a rose garden used to be. The family replanted the roses.
Winterhaven, Smith's: a poltergeist said to have moved a cast iron stove while the workmen had their backs turned.

Winton, Devonshire: said to be Kitty Love Dill, a sea captain's wife of two centuries ago. People living there in the 1960s told of sudden cold, lights on the stairs and a misty woman in a doorway. One caller swore a woman answered the telephone when nobody was home.

Spithead, Warwick: the house of the privateer Hezekiah Frith. The story is that in 1800 he brought home a young Frenchwoman taken from a prize ship and hid her in the carriage house, where she died. She is said to wander the grounds, and Frith to pace the waterfront. Noel Coward lived in the lodge in 1956.
Bel-Air, on Cobbs Hill: in 1958 a visiting theatre company held a session with a Ouija board and came away with a tale of an enslaved man tortured over stolen jewels, and a curse.
These are homes and workplaces. Please do not go looking.
In the Cathedral
A visitor on a tour of the Anglican cathedral in Hamilton was seen chatting to a wall. He said he had been introduced to a man who was repairing the building after the fire. The fire was in 1892.
Read more
John Cox's book Bermuda's Favourite Haunts is the standard collection.

sites.name: The Old Rectory and its harpsichord
sites.access: 1 Broad Alley, St George's, behind St Peter's Church. A Bermuda National Trust property. View from the lane.
sites.see: One of the oldest houses on the island.
sites.story: Built by a reformed pirate and later home to the parson. Its ghost is a polite one: people have reported the sound of a harpsichord being played softly with nobody at it.

sites.name: The Verdmont ghosts
sites.access: 6 Verdmont Lane, Smith's. A Bermuda National Trust museum. Google lists it open Monday and Thursday to Saturday, 10am to 3pm. Phone 441-236-6483.
sites.kids: A proper old house to explore by day.
sites.see: Cedar furniture, portraits and a staircase worth the visit on its own.
sites.story: Visitors reported a woman in eighteenth century dress, loud thumps with no cause, and a tall thin man who turned up several times, once in a tourist's photograph. Nothing has been reported since 1983. The writer John Cox worked here hoping to meet one and never did.
links: The Bermudian, Bermuda's Most Haunted Places
sections: The man in the attic
In August 1982 a visitor saw a man in the attic who then faded away. The Trust's first curator had seen a similar figure and took him for Spencer Joell, who lived in the house until the 1940s.

sites.name: The keeper of Gibbs Hill
sites.access: Gibbs Hill Lighthouse, Lighthouse Road. Google lists the tower open daily 10am to 4pm.
sites.kids: Climb the 185 steps and look for him at the top.
sites.see: The light, and the old keeper's cottage beside it.
sites.story: The light has run itself for years, but the ghost of a keeper long gone is said to climb up and check it anyway.
links: The Bermudian, Bermuda's Most Haunted Places
sections: The footsteps
One keeper, alone at the top with the door locked below him, heard somebody climbing the spiral stairs. His dog barked at whatever it was. Nobody came into view. Other keepers told of the same thing.

sites.name: The lady of Camden
sites.access: The Botanical Gardens, 169 South Road. Google lists the grounds open daily 6:30am to 6:30pm. The pin is the gardens, not the exact path.
sites.see: The paths around Camden, the Premier's official residence.
sites.story: On moonless nights the wife of an early Bermuda grandee, badly treated in life, is said to walk the garden paths looking to settle the score.
links: The Bermudian, Bermuda's Most Haunted Places
sections: Camden or Government House?
The Bermudian tells this same story of Government House: an early Governor's wife, ill used by her husband, heard on moonless nights as the swish of a heavy skirt. Ghost stories travel.

sites.name: The Unfinished Church
sites.access: Government Hill Road, a short walk uphill from King's Square. You look in from outside the walls.
sites.kids: A roofless stone church is a good ruin at any age.
sites.see: Gothic arches open to the sky.
sites.story: No particular ghost goes with it, but plenty of people call it haunted, and at dusk with the birds rustling in the walls it is easy to see why.

sites.name: Camping on the islands: how it works
sites.access: Two different departments run camping, with different sites, prices and ways to book.
sites.kids: Pick an island with washrooms for a first trip. Darrell's Island has them.
sites.story: There are two ways to camp in Bermuda. Four islands are run as camps by the Department of Sport and Recreation and are booked online. Three mainland and inshore sites are run by the Department of Parks and need a paper permit. Everywhere else, including the nature reserves, is off limits.
sections: The camp islands
Darrell's Island, Paget Island, White's Island and Ports Island.
Book online at sportsandrec.bm. Booking for the 2026 season opened on 6 April 2026.
In 2026 a rustic site was $60 a night and a dormitory $85 a night.
Darrell's Island has seven rustic sites and refurbished washrooms and showers, with wheelchair access. Paget Island has the Barracks for up to 50 and a cottage that sleeps 12.
The Parks sites
Ferry Point Park, Chaplin Bay, and Higgs and Horseshoe Islands.
A permit is $15 a night per campsite, from the Department of Parks at Global House, 43 Church Street, Hamilton.
The 2025 season ran from 7 May to 19 October.
Where you may not camp
Coney Island (picnics only), Blue Hole Park, Cooper's Island Nature Reserve and the dunes behind Jobson's Cove.
Nonsuch, Castle Island and the other Castle Harbour islands are nature reserves.
Private islands such as Hawkins, Marshall's and Hinson's.
A little history while you are there
Darrell's, Ports, Burt, Hawkins and Long Island were all prisoner of war camps for Boers in 1901 and 1902.
Darrell's Island was Bermuda's first airport, for flying boats, from 1936 to 1948.
Open any of those islands in this group for the story.
Rules worth knowing
An older Government page says camping is for Bermuda residents only, with no generators and no wood fires. Check the current rules when you book.
You need a boat to reach the islands.

sites.access: By boat only. A Government camp island in the Great Sound.
sites.kids: A proper island adventure: you arrive by boat and stay the night.
sites.see: Seven rustic camping areas, each named for the island's part in the early days of flying the Atlantic.
sites.story: In the Great Sound off Warwick, and owned by the Government. It has been a naval island, a quarantine station, a prison camp and Bermuda's first airport. Today it is the main Government camp island.

sections: Navy, quarantine and prisoners
Richard Norwood's map of 1621 seems to call it Captain Tucker's Island, probably after Governor Daniel Tucker.
The Royal Navy bought it with other Great Sound islands after the American War of Independence, and it served as a quarantine station.
1901 to 1902: a prisoner of war camp in the South African War. The Boers who wanted the war to go on were sent here and closely guarded.
Bermuda's first airport
1936: Imperial Airways built an air station here. There was no airfield in Bermuda, so the airliners were flying boats that landed on the Great Sound.
1937: the Cavalier service to New York began. Flying cut the journey from about 40 hours to five. Pan American shared the station, and passengers went on to Hamilton by motor boat.
1940 to 1942: the Bermuda Flying School trained Bermudian volunteers here as pilots for the Royal Air Force and the Fleet Air Arm.
In the Second World War the Royal Air Force took the island over, and transatlantic mail was landed here to be read by British censors at the Princess Hotel.
1942: Winston Churchill's Boeing flying boat used the island on his wartime Atlantic crossing.
The flying boats gave way to land planes at Kindley Field, and the island closed as an airport in 1948.
Afterwards
In the 1950s it was briefly a film location, used for the 1956 television series Crunch and Des.
Visiting today

The Bermudian magazine describes the old air base as open to the public at your own risk, with concrete buildings and hangars in decay, flat grass for camping and reefs around the shore for snorkelling.

sites.name: Paget Island
sites.era: Forts from 1612, whaling, camp island now
sites.access: By boat only, from St George's.
sites.kids: A proper island adventure: you arrive by boat and stay the night.
sites.see: Fort Cunningham, walking trails round the island and a calm lagoon about 70 yards inland.
sites.story: The 36 acre island at the mouth of St George's Harbour, named for William, fourth Lord Paget, and once known as Peniston's. It has been a fort, a whaling station, a prison camp and a boys' training school. Today it is a group camp, popular with schools, churches and youth groups.
sites.camp: Yes, by booking. The Department of Sport and Recreation runs it. Book online at sportsandrec.bm. In 2026 a rustic site was $60 a night and a dormitory $85 a night. The Barracks take up to 50 campers and a three bedroom cottage sleeps 12, with its own kitchen and bathroom.

sections: Guarding the channel

Richard Moore, the first Governor, saw in 1612 that ships bound for St George's had to pass this island, and built a fort on it. More batteries followed along the shore over the next few years, together known as Paget Fort.
In the middle of the 1700s the fort held prisoners of war. A storm wrecked much of it in 1791 and it had to be rebuilt.
Whalers
Paget and Smith's Island next door were whaling stations. Francis Forbes Hinson bought Paget Island in 1797, farmed it and hunted whales from it until the losses made him give up.
Fort Cunningham
The fort that crowns the island was rebuilt in the 1870s and named for Captain Thomas Cunningham. Its walls were faced with iron plate, which made it unlike any other fort in this half of the world.
It is part of the St George's World Heritage Site.
Prisoners, boys and campers
In the Second World War the fort was a prisoner of war camp. From 1948 into the 1960s it housed a training school for boys.
Outward Bound Bermuda has brought young people here for more than thirty years. In 2018 the Mirrors programme, Outward Bound, the Parks Department and volunteers began clearing the fort and its moat.

sites.kids: Low tide shows a sandy cove where a small boat can land.
sites.see: The Hamilton skyline from the water. Boats anchor to the west of the island.
sites.story: The small island in the middle of Hamilton Harbour, once called Hunt's Island. The United States Navy ran a base here in the last year of the First World War. Today it is one of the four Government camp islands.
sites.camp: Yes, by booking. The Department of Sport and Recreation runs it. Book online at sportsandrec.bm. In 2026 a rustic site was $60 a night and a dormitory $85 a night.

sections: A base for submarine chasers
After the American War of Independence the Admiralty bought most of the small islands in the Great Sound and Hamilton Harbour, and the Navy and the Army used White's for a century.
From 1 April 1918 it was United States Navy Base Number 24, a staging point for small anti-submarine vessels crossing the Atlantic to Europe. A supply station on Agar's Island supported it.
The base closed with a ceremony in the harbour on 1 April 1919, a year to the day after it opened.
The children's island
The Government owns it now, under the department that looks after youth and sport, and for many years it has been used by youth charities.

Generations of Bermudian children learned to swim and sail here. In 2010 the island was leased to a youth charity, and the Bermuda Sailing Association moved its youth sailing to Darrell's Island. The swimming and rowing associations kept running youth programmes on White's.
In 2013 a waterfront plan from the City of Hamilton showed a casino hotel on the island. It was never built.
A summer science station
In 1897 the American professor Charles Bristol ran a summer biological station on the island, years before Bermuda had a permanent one.

sites.name: Castle Island
sites.access: By boat only. It is part of the Castle Harbour Islands Nature Reserve, so tread lightly and check before landing.
sites.kids: Seen from a boat, or from the shore opposite.
sites.see: The ruins of King's Castle and the Devonshire Redoubt, and a sandy cove at low tide.
sites.story: The four acre island that guarded Castle Roads, the first deep channel into Bermuda. King's Castle, at its seaward end, was begun in 1612 and is the oldest surviving English fort in the New World. It gave Castle Harbour its name.
sites.camp: No. It is part of the Castle Harbour Islands Nature Reserve.
links: Wikipedia, list of islands of Bermuda
sections: Two shots in 1614

The island was first called Gurnett's Head, then King's Island. In 1612 the settlers mounted a gun here that had been salvaged from the wreck of the Sea Venture, and Governor Richard Moore soon had a proper fort built.

In 1614 a Spanish ship nosed into the channel. The gunners fired twice and missed twice, but the ship turned away. It was the only attack Spain ever made on Bermuda, and the fort had powder left for just one more shot.
What stands there
King's Castle, also called the Seaward Fort. Under Queen Anne and Queen Victoria it was the Queen's Castle.
The Captain's House of 1621, the oldest stone house in Bermuda and the oldest standing English house in the New World.
The Devonshire Redoubt of 1620 and the Landward Fort.
Later
Soldiers were back in the Second World War, living in tents inside the old walls and watching the channel with machine guns.
Since 2000 the Castle Islands forts have been part of the St George's World Heritage Site.

sites.name: Hinson's Island
sites.era: Boer War school, then Bermuda's first air base

sites.story: A residential island in the south east of the Great Sound, home to about 50 people and the only island with its own Government ferry stop. Before the houses came it held a school for boy prisoners of war and Bermuda's first seaplane hangars.
sites.camp: No. It is a residential island with private homes.

sections: Four names
Richard Norwood's survey of 1613 to 1617 recorded it as Dorrel's Island. By the middle of the 1700s it was Brown's Island.
Crown land by 1759, it was sold in 1775 to Theodore Godet for 120 pounds, and Admiralty charts of 1874 and 1894 still call it Godet Island.
A Captain Hinson bought it in the 1800s. The story goes that he lived here as a hermit after his wife died, and his name stuck.
The Khaki School
About 4,600 Boer prisoners of war were sent to Bermuda between June 1901 and January 1902. In March 1902 the Governor put Hinson's under martial law as a fourth prison zone.

It became a boarding school for the youngest prisoners, nicknamed the Khaki School. The boys were about 8 to 16 years old, many of them caught while helping older relatives at the front, and they were given lessons and taught trades. There were 180 of them in May 1902.
By August the island was empty, and martial law was lifted on 28 October. An army survey of 1903 shows two prisoner enclosures and a guard area.
Kitchener's hangars

Major Hal Kitchener, a wartime airman, nephew of Lord Kitchener and son of a Governor of Bermuda, bought the island in 1920 and built two seaplane hangars side by side. Their foundations are still there, at the spot islanders call The Slips.

This was Bermuda's first air base, run as the Bermuda and West Atlantic Aviation Company. Three Avro seaplanes took people sightseeing, by moonlight if they wished, and in October 1920 flew passengers out to watch the Prince of Wales arrive by ship. Kitchener also gave flying lessons and would loop and roll the aeroplane for anyone who paid.
His plan for a volunteer air force came to nothing. He turned the hangars into cow barns and ran a dairy, with milk bottles stamped Hinson's Island Dairy. Residents pulled down the last barn in 1955.
Houses and a ferry
A. A. Jonson bought the island from Kitchener in 1945. It was surveyed into lots of about half an acre, each with about 100 feet of shore, and a road half a mile long was laid round it.
By 1952 fifteen lots were sold, six houses were up, and the owners had formed the Hinson's Island Club to hold the shared land.
The main dock and its shelter date from the early 1950s. The Government ferry has called regularly since 1959.

Long ago it was a quarantine station, and one history of the islands says Marshall's and Burt's were each named for the person in charge of the isolation cottages there. The Royal Navy later owned it. Sir Harold Mitchell, the Scottish politician and businessman, lived here and gave it as his official address.

sections: How it became an island
Some 12,000 years ago this was a hill covered in cedar forest. As the sea rose the low ground around it turned to marsh, then to a lake, and at last to Harrington Sound.
The sound is often said to be bottomless. It is 84 feet at its deepest.
Tobacco and trunks
In the 1600s the island was rented out as farmland for tobacco, then one of Bermuda's main exports. Clearing for crops and felling cedar for timber stripped most of it bare.
Replanting was written into the lease, the first replanting on record here, and it seems to have worked.
The name may come from the stumps, or trunks, left behind when the cedars were cut for shipbuilding.
Today
The Zoological Society runs its Living Classroom here and is restoring the island's native habitat.

sections: Quarantine island
Before 1830 Burt's and Marshall's Islands were quarantine stations. Terry Tucker's book on the islands says each was named after the person who ran the isolation cottages.
In January 1830 a ship from Quebec brought smallpox to Bermuda, and an island near Turtle Cove, most likely this one or Darrell's, was offered as an isolation home.
